strengths: Clear and highly practical motivation: reducing the computational bottleneck of token-based world models during planning is a key requirement for real-time robotic application.

Simple yet effective methodology: the combination of randomized grouped attention training with inference-time random patch dropout is elegant, lightweight, and easy to integrate into existing causal transformer world models.
Extensive and diverse empirical evaluation: the paper tests the approach across six different environments involving rigid body manipulation, navigation, and deformable/granular objects.

Comprehensive baseline comparisons: the authors compare their simple random dropout strategy against several sophisticated, state-of-the-art token selection/merging approaches (e.g., STAR, LTRP, ATC) and show that simple random sampling performs comparably or better.

Insightful analytical experiments: the use of mutual information (nHSIC) and attentive probing provides a clear theoretical and empirical understanding of why random token selection is sufficient and robust.
weaknesses: The absolute planning times (reported in Table 2) are extremely high. For instance, in PushT, one iteration takes 82 seconds even at a 50% dropout rate. Given that MPC usually requires running CEM at high frequencies (e.g., 10-50 Hz), taking tens or hundreds of seconds per iteration contradicts the paper's core motivation of enabling real-time decision-making. The authors should clarify this aspect and discuss how the absolute execution time can be brought down to practical levels.

The conceptual novelty is somewhat limited. Patch dropout and attention masking are established techniques in Vision Transformers. The primary contribution here lies in applying these ideas to world model rollouts in MPC, which is more of a system-level and empirical contribution than a fundamental algorithmic breakthrough.

The performance of the model relies on the manual adjustment of the dropout fraction $p$, which varies across tasks. The paper does not offer an automated or adaptive heuristic for setting $p$ dynamically based on scene complexity or planning horizon.

The evaluation is restricted entirely to simulated environments. Deploying the model on a physical robot system would significantly strengthen the claims regarding the real-world utility of sparse imagination under real-time constraints.

strengths: The paper addresses a very practical and important bottleneck: the high computational cost of visual world models that predict rich, patch-level tokens (such as DINO-WM) during MPC-based planning.

The proposed Randomized Grouped Attention strategy during training is simple yet effective, enabling the transformer-based world model to handle arbitrary subsets of missing spatial tokens during inference.
The experimental evaluation is quite thorough, covering six diverse simulated environments including manipulation, navigation, and deformable objects.

The paper provides a detailed and honest comparative analysis against several sophisticated token selection and merging baselines (e.g., LHS, LTRP, STAR, Attention-Encoder, ATC). Finding that simple random dropout performs comparably or better is an insightful result for the community.
The manuscript is well-structured, clear, and includes good analysis (nHSIC, attentive probing, and noise robustness) to explain why sparse imagination works.
weaknesses: The primary concern is the absolute wall-clock planning latency. As shown in Table 2, even with a 50% drop ratio, a single MPC iteration takes 93 seconds in Pointmaze, 82 seconds in PushT, and 208 seconds in Block Pushing. This is extremely slow and far from real-time. The paper claims this 'paves the way for real-time decision-making,' but does not sufficiently discuss why the baseline latency is so high or how it can be realistically brought down to sub-second levels for physical robot deployment.

The architectural details of how the world model predicts future tokens are slightly vague. If the causal decoder predicts the 196 tokens auto-regressively, then dropping 50% still requires 98 sequential passes, which explains the high latency. This generation paradigm should be explicitly clarified and discussed as a limitation.

Since different random tokens are dropped at each MPC iteration, the distance to the goal (Eq. 2) is calculated over changing subsets of patches. If the random mask drops critical patches containing the target object or robot gripper, the cost function could become highly noisy or misaligned. The paper should discuss how this affects the quality of the trajectory optimization.

The absolute performance on complex tasks is quite low (e.g., Block Pushing success rate is only 22% for the Full baseline), which makes it harder to assess if the proposed method scales well to more challenging, high-precision manipulation scenarios where the base model is fully solved.

strengths: The paper addresses a highly practical bottleneck in visual world-model-based planning: the high computational cost of transformers over detailed spatial patch representations during MPC rollouts.

The proposed approach is elegant and simple, pairing randomized grouped attention during training with random token dropout during inference, avoiding the need for expensive, specialized token-selection networks.

The paper provides a commendable comparative study against several sophisticated token-reduction baselines (LHS, LTRP, Attention-Encoder, STAR, ATC), showing that simple random dropout is both more computationally efficient and performance-competitive.

Comprehensive analytical grounding is provided, including information-theoretic analysis (using normalized Hilbert-Schmidt Independence Criterion) and attentive probing to justify the information redundancy across visual tokens.
Evaluation spans six diverse simulated environments, including complex manipulation of deformable objects.
weaknesses: There is a significant gap between the 'real-time' claims in the paper and the absolute latencies reported. Table 2 shows planning times ranging from 38 to 208 seconds per iteration (MPC step). In actual robotics, real-time control usually requires 5–10 Hz (0.1–0.2 seconds per step). The paper should explicitly discuss this remaining latency gap.

It is unclear why the absolute latencies are so high. The paper should clarify if the world model rollouts during CEM are parallelized/batched. 184 seconds for 5,000 forward passes on an RTX 3090 suggests either unbatched execution or an implementation bottleneck that could be optimized.

For complex spatial tasks like PushT, the success rate degrades rapidly at higher dropout rates (e.g., dropping from 75% down to 46.7% at a 60% drop ratio). This indicates that simple random dropout is prone to discarding critical, spatially sparse details (like the exact boundaries of the T-block).

How does the target state comparison handle random dropout when computing the MPC cost? If a token corresponding to the goal's key region is dropped in the current prediction, the planning cost might ignore crucial errors. A brief discussion on how goal alignment is robustly maintained under random dropout would improve the paper.

strengths: Highly Practical and Effective Approach: The paper proposes 'sparse imagination' via random patch dropout, a simple yet highly effective way to accelerate transformer-based world model planning (e.g., achieving ~50% latency reduction) without sacrificing control performance.

Innovative Training Strategy: The 'Randomized Grouped Attention' strategy successfully trains the world model to handle arbitrary token subsets, proving critical for maintaining low prediction error on sparse inputs.

Extensive and Diverse Benchmarking: The evaluation spans eight simulator tasks (including complex environments with deformable objects, LIBERO-10, and Meta-World) as well as real-world robotic manipulation using a physical SO-101 robot arm.

Deconstructive and Insightful Analysis: The paper provides a very insightful explanation of why simple random sampling outperforms complex, state-of-the-art token pruning methods. The discovery and quantitative analysis of the 'Blind Spot' problem of static, importance-based metrics in dynamic environments is a significant scientific contribution.

Excellent Clarity and Transparency: The manuscript is exceptionally well-written, with high-quality visualizations (e.g., the blind-spot illustration in Figure 9) and a detailed appendix covering execution time breakdown, noise robustness, and implementation parameters.
weaknesses: Comparison with simpler training-time dropout: The paper introduces Randomized Grouped Attention to train the world model. It would strengthen the ablation to compare this specifically against a simpler training baseline where a random percentage of tokens are simply dropped entirely from the sequence (rather than grouped and processed via masked attention).

Sensitivity to Hyperparameter p: While the paper shows 50% is a robust default, the choice of the optimal dropout ratio still seems somewhat heuristic and task-dependent. The preliminary adaptive methods (Ada-Rand/Ada-Inc) in the appendix do not outperform the fixed ratio, leaving room for future work on automated dynamic selection.

Dependency on Pre-trained Encoders: The efficacy of the approach is tightly coupled to the spatial features and redundancy of pre-trained encoders (like DINO-ViT). In scenarios where the pre-trained visual representation is less redundant or less descriptive, performance under high dropout rates might degrade more rapidly.

strengths: Highly practical and relevant motivation: Visual world models that predict spatial patch tokens (like DINO-WM) suffer from quadratic complexity in self-attention, making real-time planning extremely challenging. This paper addresses a highly critical bottleneck for robot control.

Simple and elegant solution: The proposed 'Sparse Imagination' is simple, training the world model with randomized grouped attention and performing inference with random token dropout. It introduces near-zero computational overhead during the selection process.

Insightful analysis of the 'Blind Spot' problem: The paper provides a highly compelling, counter-intuitive insight explaining why simple random sampling consistently outperforms sophisticated importance-based pruning or clustering methods. Importance-based methods are static and systematically ignore areas that later become dynamic and critical during planning. This is backed by solid quantitative and qualitative proof (e.g., Table 12 and Figure 9).

Extensive and rigorous evaluation: The method is validated on a large suite of tasks, including six standard simulators, LIBERO-10, Meta-World, and real-world SO-101 robotic manipulation tasks (PickPlace and Drawer) guided by a VLA model.

Thorough ablations and analysis: The paper includes a wide range of analytical experiments, such as generalization across different vision encoders (MoCo-v3, MAE, DINOv3), robustness to noise, gradient-based planning compatibility, and uncertainty-aware adaptive dropout.
weaknesses: Statistical significance in small evaluation sets: For some complex simulation environments, the number of evaluation episodes is quite small (e.g., 20 evaluations for Granular, 30 for Rope). Since random dropout and planning are naturally stochastic, these small sample sizes can introduce high variance. Providing confidence intervals or running more evaluation trials would make the results in Table 1 more robust.

Absolute computational bottleneck of CEM: Even with a 50% token dropout, the absolute planning times for standard MPC-CEM in Table 2 are still very high (e.g., 109 seconds per iteration for PushT). While VLA-guided planning successfully bypasses this by evaluating pre-filtered action chunks, the paper should more clearly clarify that standard CEM remains too slow for real-time robotic feedback loops, and that VLA guidance is the key enabler for physical deployment.

Clarity on Figure 4: The caption of Figure 4 mentions 'various drop ratios', but the bar chart shows only a single pair of bars per environment. The authors should specify which exact drop ratio (e.g., 50%) is being visualized.

strengths: The paper addresses a very practical and crucial bottleneck in visual world model planning: the quadratic computational complexity associated with processing a large number of spatial tokens.

The proposed approach is elegant and remarkably simple, combining random token dropout during planning with a randomized grouped attention mechanism during training. This avoids any complex ranking or clustering overhead during inference.
Extensive and thorough experiments across eight simulation environments (including complex ones like LIBERO-10 and Meta-World) and two real-world robotic manipulation tasks with a SO-101 arm.

The paper provides a highly insightful analysis explaining why simple random dropout outperforms sophisticated importance-based pruning methods, introducing the concept of the 'blind spot' problem in dynamic planning.
The paper is exceptionally well-written, clearly illustrated, and supported by a robust set of ablations (including noise robustness analysis, runtime profiling, and adaptive dropout mechanisms).
weaknesses: The proposed method requires retraining the world model with the randomized grouped attention strategy. While this is a one-time cost, it means the technique cannot be directly applied post-hoc to existing pre-trained transformer world models without fine-tuning or retraining.

The evaluation lacks comparison with dynamic, motion-aware token selection methods (e.g., selecting tokens based on optical flow or temporal difference) which would be the natural counter-strategy to resolve the static 'blind spot' problem.

While the planning speedup is significant, the absolute latency of VLA-guided planning (even with 50% drop) remains high compared to direct policy execution, which may still limit its applicability in high-frequency closed-loop control tasks.
